rationale: A wins because it mostly keeps its hands on the evidence and names the proof gates before a reporter can kill the pitch. Its “Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike” is a clean data story tied to the actual missing proof, while B poisons an otherwise sharp set with “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them,” which the update does not say. B is smarter on the adjusted-EBITDA/net-loss tension, but one confidently false business-model headline is not strategy; it is a fact-check failure with formatting.
gaps_in_A: “The company everyone wrote off” and “The prevailing belief is that pandemic-era connected-fitness winners are in permanent decline” import a media consensus that is not in the update. Cite prior coverage or cut the swagger.

“first profitable quarter” is defensible because the update says it, but the angle needs the adjusted-EBITDA/free-cash-flow caveat in the headline or first sentence; the net-loss/debt caveat cannot live only in the proof list.
“Inside the $200M cost-cutting playbook” is promising but under-built. Without the CEO’s name, access, and a breakdown of the cuts, it is a profile-shaped IOU.
gaps_in_B: “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them” is invented. The update says Peloton is expanding rental nationwide, not replacing sales.
“$2,000+ upfront purchase” and “The $2,000 bike is now a monthly bill” import price facts not supplied in the update. In a blind grounding test, that is not color; it is leakage.

The second and fourth angles both ride the same rental expansion: “Peloton stopped selling bikes…” and “The $2,000 bike is now a monthly bill…”. The customer lens is plausible, but it needs an actual renter or it reads like padded duplication.
“category-creation” overstates the move. A low-cost national rental rollout is a business-model angle; calling it category creation makes the suit too shiny.
